title: Emotional Expressions Reconsidered: Challenges to Inferring Emotion From Human Facial Movements
authors: Barrett, L. F.; Adolphs, R.; Marsella, S.; Martinez, A. M.; Pollak, S. D.
key_findings: Tests the 'common view' that anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise can be read from facial configurations; evidence does not support using them as diagnostic of emotion.
Four criteria: reliability, specificity, generalizability, validity.
People do scowl/smile/frown more than chance in the matching emotion, but the link is weak: meta-analysis cited (Duran et al. 2017) average r = .32, average proportion .19 (category range .15-.25).
Posed expressions match the prototypes better than spontaneous ones; e.g. only 8 of 55 winning judo fighters produced a Duchenne smile (Study 1), all during social interaction.
Context (situation, culture, internal state) is largely unmeasured and is a likely reason for weak reliability; automated detectors drop below ~83% accuracy outside the lab.
practical_applications: Rule for the studio: never state or caption a character's inner emotion from face or voice alone; give context (situation, words, action).
Faceless Mint & Tao fit this science: emotion is carried by situation, posture and dialogue, not a stereotyped face.
limitations: Only the first ~100k of ~560k characters of the PMC page were read; the closing recommendations section was not read in full.
Critics from basic-emotion tradition dispute how strongly to read the results (not reviewed here).

title: The theory of constructed emotion: an active inference account of interoception and categorization
key_findings: Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience 12(1). Presents the theory of constructed emotion (formerly the conceptual act theory) as a brain-based computational account.
The brain uses prediction (predictive coding) and interoception, and categorizes sensations with learned emotion concepts to construct instances of emotion.
Emotion categories show degeneracy: dissimilar brain representations can produce instances of the same category, so no one-to-one emotion-circuit mapping is expected.
practical_applications: Supports showing emotion through situation + concept (words, culture) rather than fixed facial templates.
Explains why Thai emotion words (jai-compounds) may shape what viewers feel and name.
limitations: PMC full text blocked by a browser check this session; content known only from search summaries and Wikipedia.
Published online Oct 2016 in SCAN 12(1); page range differs between sources (Ovid lists 1-23).

title: Appraisal Theories of Emotion: State of the Art and Future Development
authors: Moors, A.; Ellsworth, P. C.; Scherer, K. R.; Frijda, N. H.
key_findings: Appraisal theories define emotions as processes (episodes), not states; componential: appraisal, motivational (action tendencies), somatic, motor (expression) and feeling components.
The process is continuous and recursive; changes in one component feed back to others; several episodes may run in parallel.
Appraisal detects significance for well-being = satisfaction/obstruction of concerns (needs, attachments, values, goals, beliefs).

Core appraisal variables: goal relevance, goal congruence, certainty, agency (self/other/circumstance), coping potential/control; some add novelty, urgency, intentionality, fairness, norm compatibility.
practical_applications: Write story beats as appraisal changes: same event, different appraisal -> different emotion (e.g. Tao blames himself = guilt; blames the shop = anger).
Use the appraisal variables as a checklist when designing a turning point in a carousel.
limitations: Introduction to a special section; summarises rather than tests theories.
Appraisal lists are not claimed to be exhaustive or universal.

title: The dynamic architecture of emotion: Evidence for the component process model
key_findings: Emotion as an emergent dynamic process based on subjective appraisal of significant events; emphasis on the sequence of appraisal checks (stimulus evaluation checks) and synchronisation of response systems.
practical_applications: Sequence for a reaction shot: novelty -> pleasantness -> goal relevance -> coping -> norms; animate the change in that order.
limitations: Only abstract and secondary descriptions seen.

title: Cognition and Motivation in Emotion
key_findings: American Psychologist 46(4), 352-367.
Primary appraisal (is this relevant to my well-being: harm/benefit) and secondary appraisal (coping options).
Core relational themes summarise the emotion-producing person-environment relation, e.g. anger: unfairly slighted; anxiety: anticipated harm with doubt about coping; shame: personal failure.
practical_applications: One-line 'core relational theme' per scene makes the intended emotion explicit for writers and voice directors.
limitations: Read via an HTML copy hosted on a university site; themes for envy, pride, hope etc. are in the 1991 book, not this article.

title: Appraisal in the Emotion System: Coherence in Strategies for Coping
key_findings: Emotion Review 5(2), 141-149. Emotions form an organised system of coping strategies guided by appraisals, for threats and opportunities.
practical_applications: Frame each emotion by what it makes the character DO (coping strategy), useful for action beats.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: An argument for basic emotions
key_findings: Emotions evolved for adaptive value; characteristics include rapid onset, short duration, unbidden occurrence, automatic appraisal and coherence among responses.
Emotion 'families' share expression, physiology, antecedents and perhaps appraisal.
practical_applications: Basic-emotion families are still a useful coarse index for libraries (joy, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise).
limitations: The PDF link returned 404 this session; content from abstract and secondary summaries.
Strong universality claims contested (Barrett2019, Jack2012).

title: Core affect and the psychological construction of emotion
key_findings: Core affect = neurophysiological state consciously accessible as the simplest raw feeling; a single blend of pleasure-displeasure and activation (a point on the circumplex).

Core affect can be free-floating (mood) or attributed to an Object, beginning an emotional episode; prototypical episodes such as fear/anger = core affect attributed to something plus non-emotional processes.
Defines affective quality (a stimulus' power to change core affect), attributed affect, affect regulation, emotional meta-experience.
practical_applications: Images/clips set core affect (pleasant/calm etc.) through 'affective quality'; the caption/dialogue supplies the Object that turns it into a named emotion.
Explains 'mood' entries (visual.coziness) as affective quality, not character emotion.
limitations: Read via text extraction of a course-hosted PDF copy (keyword excerpts).

title: Pleasure-arousal-dominance: A general framework for describing and measuring individual differences in temperament
key_findings: Current Psychology 14, 261-292. Three nearly orthogonal dimensions (pleasure, arousal, dominance) describe emotional states; temperament = average emotional state across situations.
practical_applications: Dominance axis separates anger (high D) from fear (low D) at the same valence/arousal - useful for posture and camera height.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries only.

title: Self-report captures 27 distinct categories of emotion bridged by continuous gradients
key_findings: PNAS 114(38), E7900-E7909. Reported emotional states elicited by 2,185 short videos.
Videos reliably elicited 27 distinct varieties of reported emotional experience; category labels (e.g. amusement) captured reports better than valence/arousal dimensions.

Boundaries between categories are fuzzy, linked by gradients (anxiety-fear-horror-disgust; calmness-aesthetic appreciation-awe) that track smooth variation in dimensions such as valence and dominance.
practical_applications: Reference list for gap analysis of the studio's emotion libraries.
Gradients suggest designing transitions along neighbouring states, not jumps.
limitations: Abstract-level; US English-speaking sample; Barrett et al. published a constructionist reply.

title: The brain basis of emotion: A meta-analytic review
authors: Lindquist, K. A.; Wager, T. D.; Kober, H.; Bliss-Moreau, E.; Barrett, L. F.
key_findings: Behavioral and Brain Sciences 35(3), 121-143. Meta-analytic summary of human neuroimaging studies of emotion experience and perception.
Little evidence that discrete emotion categories are consistently and specifically localized to distinct brain regions (locationist hypothesis).
Evidence fits psychological construction: a set of interacting, domain-general networks is active across emotion categories and in non-emotional operations.
practical_applications: Science basis for treating emotion labels as useful categories, not brain modules.
limitations: Findings not read this session; only the framing from search results.

title: Emotion (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Three traditions: feeling, evaluative (incl. appraisal), motivational.
Basic emotion theory vs psychological constructionism; appraisal theories answer the differentiation problem via appraisal patterns but do not by themselves say what emotions are.
practical_applications: Orientation map for writers choosing which theory to lean on for a given task.
limitations: Read first ~100k characters plus footer; first published 25 Sep 2018, revision date not seen.

title: Putting the Self Into Self-Conscious Emotions: A Theoretical Model
authors: Tracy, J. L.; Robins, R. W.
key_findings: Psychological Inquiry 15(2), 103-125. Self-conscious emotions require self-awareness and self-representations, emerge later, are cognitively complex and show weaker evidence of universal expressions.
Model: attention to self -> identity-goal relevance -> internal attribution; shame = internal stable/global ('I'm a dumb person'), guilt = internal unstable/specific ('I didn't try hard enough').
Embarrassment: public self, identity-goal incongruence, internal attribution; argued less cognitively elaborated, emerges earlier in childhood.
Two prides: achievement-oriented (unstable/specific) vs hubristic (stable/global). Humiliation proposed as public focus + stable/global blame (flagged as under-researched).
practical_applications: Write shame vs guilt lines by the attribution: 'I'm hopeless' (shame) vs 'I forgot your glasses' (guilt).
Pride beats: credit the effort ('I practised') not the self ('I'm the best') to keep a character likeable.
limitations: Read via text extraction of a course-hosted copy (keyword excerpts).
Theoretical model; predictions tested later by others.

title: Moral emotions and moral behavior
authors: Tangney, J. P.; Stuewig, J.; Mashek, D. J.
key_findings: Annual Review of Psychology 58, 345-372. Reviews shame, guilt, embarrassment and positive moral emotions (elevation, gratitude, pride), plus other-oriented empathy.
Self-conscious emotions function as an 'emotional moral barometer' and can be anticipated before acting as well as felt afterwards.
On balance guilt (about a behaviour) appears more adaptive than shame (about the self); guilt-proneness consistently correlates with perspective-taking and empathic concern.
practical_applications: Guilt (repair) is the prosocial self-conscious emotion; brand stories should invite repair, never shame the viewer.
limitations: Only abstract-level summaries read (PMC blocked).

title: Signs of Appeasement: Evidence for the Distinct Displays of Embarrassment, Amusement, and Shame
key_findings: JPSP 68(3), 441-454. Five studies: embarrassment has a distinct nonverbal display that differs from amusement and is identified by observers.
Embarrassment markers: gaze down, gaze shifts, smile controls, head turn, face touches; nearly all embarrassed targets looked down (94% vs 72% of amused).
Appeasement hypothesis: display more readily perceived from lower-status individuals.
practical_applications: Animate embarrassment as a 2-3 s sequence (look down -> suppressed smile -> head turn -> touch face) for faceless puppets via body and head.
limitations: Lab sample, US students; display is a tendency not a diagnostic (see Barrett2019).
Read via text extraction (keyword excerpts).

title: Approaching awe, a moral, spiritual, and aesthetic emotion
key_findings: Cognition and Emotion 17, 297-314. Prototype approach: perceived vastness + need for accommodation; peripheral flavours.
Proposed evolutionary origin in low-rank members' response to powerful leaders.
practical_applications: Awe images need scale (small figure, vast scene) and something that does not fit expectations.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries; theoretical paper.

title: The Science of Awe (white paper for the John Templeton Foundation)
authors: Allen, S. (Greater Good Science Center, UC Berkeley)
key_findings: Summarises Keltner & Haidt: vastness + accommodation; five flavours: threat, beauty, ability, virtue, supernatural causality.
Awe often accompanied by 'small self', connectedness; cultural differences in elicitors (personal accomplishment more in US, awe of another person more in China).
practical_applications: Threat-flavoured awe (storm, huge wave) vs beauty awe (sunset at Hua Hin) need different palettes and music.
limitations: Funded white paper, narrative review; read via text extraction (excerpts).

title: Awe, the small self, and prosocial behavior
authors: Piff, P. K.; Dietze, P.; Feinberg, M.; Stancato, D. M.; Keltner, D.
key_findings: JPSP 108(6). Five studies; dispositional and induced awe linked to more prosocial behaviour, mediated by a sense of small self (per press release).
practical_applications: Awe scenes can precede a kindness beat in a story.
limitations: Press-release level; a student replication reported failure to replicate the small-self finding (unpublished).

title: The relationship between awe and prosocial behavior: Three-level meta-analysis and meta-analytic structural equation modeling
authors: Lin, R.; Yu, Q.; Hu, T.; Zhang, J.; Ye, Y.; Lian, R.
key_findings: Acta Psychologica Sinica 57(4), 631-651. Subgroup estimates seen in snippets: self-report prosocial measures r ~ .41, lab behavioural measures r ~ .24.
practical_applications: Expect awe->kindness effects to be modest in real behaviour.
limitations: Pooled estimate not seen; snippet-level only.

title: Find, Remind, and Bind: The Functions of Gratitude in Everyday Relationships
key_findings: Social and Personality Psychology Compass 6(6), 455-469. Gratitude helps find new relationship partners, reminds of existing ones and binds (maintains) them.
practical_applications: Thank-you posts to customers work as relationship 'bind' moments, not just politeness.
limitations: Secondary summaries only.

title: Leveling up and down: The experiences of benign and malicious envy
authors: van de Ven, N.; Zeelenberg, M.; Pieters, R.
key_findings: Emotion 9(3), 419-429. Benign envy -> moving-up motivation (self-improvement); malicious envy -> pulling-down motivation; found in Dutch (two words) and US/Spanish (one word) samples.
practical_applications: Marketing should evoke benign envy (I could have that too) and never malicious envy or mockery of others.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Emotional Contagion
authors: Hatfield, E.; Cacioppo, J. T.; Rapson, R. L.
key_findings: Current Directions in Psychological Science 2(3). Primitive emotional contagion: automatic mimicry of face, voice, posture, then feedback from the mimicry shapes one's own feeling, producing convergence (as summarised by secondary sources).
practical_applications: A calm, warm narrator voice and relaxed body language in clips are the low-level route to a calm viewer.
limitations: Full text behind login; mechanism details from secondary summaries.

title: A multi-lab test of the facial feedback hypothesis by the Many Smiles Collaboration
key_findings: Nature Human Behaviour 6, 1731-1742. Preregistered adversarial multi-lab study, n = 3,878 participants in 19 countries.
Facial mimicry and voluntary facial action tasks could both amplify and initiate feelings of happiness.
Evidence was less conclusive when facial feedback was manipulated unobtrusively via the pen-in-mouth task.
practical_applications: Feedback (part of contagion) is real but small: do not promise 'smile and you will feel happy' in health content.
limitations: Effect sizes not read this session.
Only the abstract on the publisher page was read (full text paywalled at session time).

title: Experimental evidence of massive-scale emotional contagion through social networks
authors: Kramer, A. D. I.; Guillory, J. E.; Hancock, J. T.
key_findings: PNAS 111(24), 8788-8790. News Feed experiment with N = 689,003 Facebook users.
Reducing positive posts: positive words in users' updates fell by 0.1% (d = 0.02) and negative words rose 0.04% (d = 0.001); reducing negative posts had the opposite pattern (d = 0.02 and 0.008).
Authors note effects are small (as small as d = 0.001) but argue they matter at scale; a withdrawal effect also appeared (fewer emotional posts seen -> less expressive).
practical_applications: Feed tone spreads in text form even without faces; keep the shop's feed warm, not anxious.
limitations: Effect sizes very small (not verified here); Editorial Expression of Concern over consent - ethically contested.
Effect sizes are tiny; consent/ethics of the experiment were widely criticised (secondary).
PNAS published an Editorial Expression of Concern (111(29):10779) about consent.
Spot-check U3 2026-11-25 applied.

title: The emerging field of emotion regulation: An integrative review
key_findings: Review of General Psychology 2(3), 271-299. Defines emotion regulation as how people influence which emotions they have, when, and how they experience and express them; distinguishes it from coping, mood regulation, defence and affect regulation.

Process model: antecedent-focused strategies (situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change/reappraisal) vs response-focused strategies (response modulation, e.g. suppression).
Reviews early evidence that reappraisal and suppression have different consequences, with reappraisal acting earlier in the emotion process.
practical_applications: Five regulation points = five places a story character can change an emotion: choose the situation, change it, shift attention, rethink it, hide it.
limitations: Abstract-level; full text not read.

title: Emotion regulation: Affective, cognitive, and social consequences
key_findings: Psychophysiology 39(3), 281-291. Reappraisal (early) decreases experience and expression with no memory cost; suppression (late) decreases expression but not experience, impairs memory and increases physiological responding for suppressors and their partners.
Suppressing negative expression does not reduce negative experience, but suppressing positive expression does reduce amusement.
practical_applications: 'Holding back tears' = suppression: the feeling stays, the body leaks (breath, jaw, hands).
Reappraisal lines ('maybe it's a chance to...') are the healthy turn in Mint & Tao stories.
limitations: Read via text extraction of a course-hosted PDF (abstract + excerpts); mostly US student samples.

title: Individual differences in two emotion regulation processes: Implications for affect, relationships, and well-being
authors: Gross, J. J.; John, O. P.
key_findings: JPSP 85(2), 348-362. Five studies; introduces the ERQ. Habitual reappraisal relates to better well-being and interpersonal functioning; habitual suppression to worse.
practical_applications: Characters who habitually suppress can be shown as more distant in relationships - a gentle arc toward sharing feelings.
limitations: Correlational; abstract only.

title: Emotion Regulation: Current Status and Future Prospects
key_findings: Psychological Inquiry 26(1), 1-26. Extended process model: regulation as valuation with stages identification, selection, implementation.
practical_applications: Story arcs of regulation: notice the feeling -> pick a strategy -> carry it out.
limitations: Search summaries only; commentary notes co-regulation is underplayed.

title: Dealing with feeling: A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of strategies derived from the process model of emotion regulation
authors: Webb, T. L.; Miles, E.; Sheeran, P.
key_findings: Psychological Bulletin 138(4), 775-808. 306 comparisons: attentional deployment overall d+ = 0.00 (distraction 0.27, concentration -0.26); response modulation small (0.16; suppressing expression 0.32, suppressing experience/thoughts not effective); cognitive change small-medium (reappraising stimulus 0.36, perspective taking 0.45, reappraising response 0.23).
practical_applications: Perspective-taking is the strongest listed strategy - ideal for Mint helping Tao see it from another side.
limitations: Figures from abstract/secondary snippets; lab manipulations.

title: Emotion regulation and culture: Are the social consequences of emotion suppression culture-specific?
authors: Butler, E. A.; Lee, T. L.; Gross, J. J.
key_findings: Emotion 7(1), 30-48. Suppression's negative social effects (less responsiveness, hostile partner perceptions) were smaller for participants with stronger Asian values.
practical_applications: Thai polite restraint should not automatically be written as cold or fake; in-culture it can read as considerate.
limitations: Female US college students (European vs bicultural Asian values); not Thai samples.

title: Unpacking Emotion Differentiation: Transforming Unpleasant Experience by Perceiving Distinctions in Negativity
authors: Kashdan, T. B.; Barrett, L. F.; McKnight, P. E.
key_findings: Current Directions in Psychological Science 24, 10-16. Emotion differentiation (granularity) - distinguishing fine-grained negative states - supports regulation and is a component of interventions.
practical_applications: Precise emotion words in Thai captions (e.g. 'น้อยใจ' vs 'เสียใจ') are more useful to viewers than 'sad'.
limitations: Abstract-level; measurement validity debated.

title: Eliciting mixed emotions: a meta-analysis comparing models, types, and measures
authors: Berrios, R.; Totterdell, P.; Kellett, S.
key_findings: 63 experimental studies (N = 7,157): mixed emotions reliably elicited, d = 0.77 (PET-PEESE corrected ~0.53); similar across discrete vs dimensional models and across mixed-emotion types.
Happy-sad is the most studied pair; methods include films, music, ads, autobiographical recall.
Supports the Evaluative Space Model (positive and negative affect as separable) over strictly bipolar circumplex.
practical_applications: Bittersweet endings (farewell, last day of a season) are a scientifically real target, not a contradiction.
limitations: Experimental studies only; self-report and memory biases; first ~100k characters read.

title: Which emotions last longest and why: The role of event importance and rumination
key_findings: Motivation and Emotion 39, 119-127. 233 Belgian high-school students recalled recent episodes of 27 emotions and reported duration, appraisals and regulation.
Sadness lasted longest (median ~120 h in the paper's figure); shame, surprise, fear, disgust, boredom, being touched, irritation and relief were shortest.
Fear was shorter than anxiety (t(1647) = 4.12, p < .0001) and guilt longer than shame (t(1647) = 2.71, p = .0067).
Event importance and rumination together accounted for 43% of the between-emotion variance in duration.
practical_applications: Sadness/guilt beats can linger across slides; fear/surprise resolve fast.
limitations: Retrospective self-report; Belgian adolescents; specific hour figures from press coverage only.
Retrospective self-reports from one adolescent sample; the press figure of ~35 h for joy was not confirmed from the text.

title: Emotion dynamics
key_findings: Current Opinion in Psychology 17, 22-26. Study of trajectories, patterns and regularities of emotional change over time; inertia (resistance to change) cited from this line of work.
practical_applications: Character design: high-inertia character (slow to change mood) vs high-variability character.
limitations: Bibliographic record + citing papers only.

title: Duration neglect in retrospective evaluations of affective episodes
key_findings: JPSP 65(1), 45-55. Study 1: 32 participants rated pleasant and aversive film clips of varied length in real time and globally; Study 2: 96 participants ranked the clips from memory or online.
Effects of duration on retrospective evaluations were small, fully explained by changes in real-time affect, and smaller when made from memory (duration neglect).

Retrospective evaluations behave like a weighted average of 'snapshots'; the paper cites a reanalysis of Varey & Kahneman (1992) where peak + end discomfort explained 94% of variance and duration added only 3%.
practical_applications: Design every clip and carousel with a deliberate peak and a warm last slide; length matters less than the ending.
limitations: Lab film clips; peak-end does not hold well for day-long experiences (Miron-Shatz).
The 94% figure comes from the cited reanalysis of judgments about another person's schematic discomfort reports, not from these film studies.

title: Cognitive neuroscience of emotional memory
key_findings: Nature Reviews Neuroscience 7(1), 54-64. The amygdala mediates emotional learning and boosts memory operations in hippocampus and prefrontal cortex across encoding, consolidation and retrieval.
practical_applications: Emotional (arousing) moments in a story are remembered better - put the product/brand inside the emotional beat, not after it.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Confidence, not consistency, characterizes flashbulb memories
authors: Talarico, J. M.; Rubin, D. C.
key_findings: Psychological Science 14(5), 455-461. 54 students after 9/11: consistency of flashbulb and everyday memories declined equally; only vividness/confidence stayed high for flashbulb memories.
practical_applications: Emotional memories feel vivid but are not more accurate: characters can be confidently wrong about the past - a good story device.
limitations: Small sample; up to 32 weeks.

title: Facial expressions of emotion are not culturally universal
authors: Jack, R. E.; Garrod, O. G. B.; Yu, H.; Caldara, R.; Schyns, P. G.
key_findings: PNAS 109(19), 7241-7244. Reverse-correlation with a generative face grammar: 15 Western Caucasian and 15 East Asian observers each categorized 4,800 animations.
Western mental models formed six distinct clusters for the six 'basic' emotions; East Asian models did not form distinct clusters.
East Asian observers represented emotional intensity with distinctive dynamic eye activity; authors argue this refutes the universality hypothesis.
practical_applications: Do not rely on Western-coded facial clichés for Thai audiences; context matters more.
limitations: Debated (Sauter & Eisner comment and reply); summaries only.
Small observer sample (30); later critiques (e.g. Sauter & Eisner, secondary) dispute the strength of the conclusion.

title: The fear gasping face as a threat display in a Melanesian society
authors: Crivelli, C.; Russell, J. A.; Jarillo, S.; Fernández-Dols, J.-M.
key_findings: PNAS 113(44). Two studies with adolescents of the Trobriand Islands (Papua New Guinea), with researchers speaking the vernacular.
Study 1: mixed, variable attribution with much lower agreement than in Western samples; the gasping 'fear' face was consistently matched to anger and threat.
Study 2: asked to pick the threatening face, Trobrianders chose the gasping 'fear' face, Spaniards the scowling 'angry' face.
practical_applications: Face-to-emotion mappings are culture-dependent.
limitations: Small-scale society; definitional critique of 'gasping face'.

title: On the universality and cultural specificity of emotion recognition: a meta-analysis
key_findings: Psychological Bulletin 128(2), 203-235. Emotions recognised above chance across cultures, with an in-group advantage (better accuracy for same-culture expressors).
practical_applications: Thai actors/voices are read more accurately by Thai viewers - favour Thai talent and Thai TTS.
limitations: Matsumoto (2002) disputes the in-group advantage on design grounds.

title: Cultural variations in emotions: A review
key_findings: Psychological Bulletin 112(2), 179-204. Cultural differences and similarities appear in every phase of the emotion process; which appears depends on level of description; differences arise from event schemas, appraisal propensities, behaviour repertoires, regulation.
practical_applications: Localise emotion at each phase: what triggers it in Thai life, how it is appraised, how it is shown, how it is regulated.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Emotion semantics show both cultural variation and universal structure
authors: Jackson, J. C.; Watts, J.; Henry, T. R.; List, J.-M.; et al.
key_findings: Science 366(6472), 1517-1522. Colexification analysis of emotion concepts across 2,474 spoken languages.
Emotion colexification networks vary significantly across language families, and the variation is predicted by the geographic proximity of the families.
Universal structure too: all families differentiate emotions primarily by hedonic valence and secondarily by physiological activation.
practical_applications: Translate emotions by meaning, not word-for-word; valence/arousal is the safe common ground.
limitations: Abstract/press-level.

title: Cultural variation in affect valuation
authors: Tsai, J. L.; Knutson, B.; Fung, H. H.
key_findings: JPSP. Ideal affect (how people want to feel) is shaped by culture more than actual affect; European Americans value high-arousal positive states more, Hong Kong Chinese value low-arousal positive (calm) more; a 2025 meta-analysis reports these differences persist.
practical_applications: Thai/Asian audiences may respond to calm-positive (LAP) imagery; test rather than assume.
limitations: No Thai samples; secondary summaries.

title: A comparative study of smiling facial expressions and display rules of the Thai and the Japanese
key_findings: Asian Review 29(1), 101-121. Interviews: when not happy, Thais smiled more when greeting or apologising; Japanese smiled more to fit in with a group; Thais raised cheeks (AU6) more when smiling with sadness.
practical_applications: A Thai smile in a story is a social act (greeting, apology, kreng jai), not proof of joy.
limitations: Abstract only; sample size not seen.

title: A discourse analysis of the Thai experience of 'being krengjai'
key_findings: Intercultural Pragmatics. Historical research + questionnaire of 471 Thai people mapping the many meanings of krengjai (consideration, deference, reluctance to impose).
practical_applications: Kreng jai lines need a relational context (status gap, debt, closeness).
limitations: Publisher page returned an error; known from search summary only.

title: Psychology of the Thai People: Values and Behavioral Patterns
key_findings: Bangkok: NIDA. Nine Thai value clusters from a survey of 2,469 Thais (1978-81), including interdependence and fun-pleasure (sanuk) orientations (per secondary sources).
practical_applications: Sanuk and interdependence as content tones for the shop.
limitations: Not read; year given as 1990 or 1991 in different records.

title: Basic Emotion Words Derived from Physiological Effects in Thai
authors: ต๊ะวิชัย ศ. (as listed on the journal page)
key_findings: Journal of the Faculty of Arts, Silpakorn University 37(2), 182-221. 195 Thai basic emotion words from the Royal Institute Dictionary 2011 + survey of 200 speakers; prototypes include ชื่นใจ (happiness), ต้องใจ (affection), น้ำตาตกใน (sorrow), เสียวสันหลัง (fear), เลือดพล่าน (anger); seven lexicalisation processes; meaning extended via metonymy/metaphor.
practical_applications: Use bodily Thai idioms in captions and VO for vivid, culturally native emotion naming.
limitations: Abstract only; issue labelled 2015 but published online 2020.

title: A Review of Studies in Heart or Jai Metaphor in Thai Language
key_findings: Manutsat Paritat: Journal of Humanities 45(2), 68-85. Jai (heart) metaphors fall into four groups: heart as person, object, space, container; central to everyday Thai emotion talk.
practical_applications: Visual metaphors for Thai emotion (a 'cool' or 'wide' heart) can be drawn from these mappings.
limitations: Abstract only; DOI shown on page looked malformed, omitted.

title: Assessing Equanimity in a Thai Buddhist Context: Psychometric Validation of the Thai Equanimity Scale-16
key_findings: Journal of Socio-Buddhist Analytics 11(1), 162-175 (Jan-Mar 2026). Thai Equanimity Scale-16 validated with 437 Thai mindfulness-oriented adults; 211 from monastic-university networks retested after one week.
Two-factor model (Experiential Acceptance, Non-Reactivity) fit well: CFI = 0.994, TLI = 0.990, RMSEA = 0.020; internal consistency .84; one-week test-retest r = .89.

Higher equanimity associated with greater benevolence and fewer aversive tendencies (SOFI); authors argue Western scales reduce upekkha to emotion regulation/reduced reactivity, missing its insight- and compassion-based meaning.
practical_applications: 'Jai yen'/equanimity is valued in Thai culture and is more than suppression.
limitations: Search snippet only; authors not captured.
Sample is mindfulness-oriented Thai adults, not the general public.

title: Thai Culture: Core Concepts (The Cultural Atlas)
key_findings: Describes face, hierarchy, harmony (calm demeanour, avoiding outbursts), sanuk (finding enjoyment in what one does) linked to 'mai pen rai'.
practical_applications: Background for tone; not evidence about emotion processes.
limitations: Cultural guide, no in-text citations; generalises a diverse country.
